learningObjectives.title: Nazi Germany: control and daily life

questions.q: In which year did Kaiser Wilhelm II abdicate, leading to the creation of the Weimar Republic?
questions.explain: The Kaiser abdicated in November 1918 as Germany faced defeat and revolution, allowing a republic to be declared.

questions.q: Who became the first President of the Weimar Republic in 1919?
options: Friedrich Ebert
Paul von Hindenburg
Gustav Stresemann
Philipp Scheidemann
questions.explain: The Social Democrat Friedrich Ebert was the Republic's first President, serving until his death in 1925.

questions.q: What power did Article 48 of the Weimar Constitution give the President?
options: The right to rule by decree in an emergency without the Reichstag's consent
The power to abolish all political parties
The right to appoint judges for life
The power to declare war without any consultation
questions.explain: Article 48 let the President bypass parliament in an emergency, a power later exploited to undermine democracy.

questions.q: Why is proportional representation often blamed for the Weimar Republic's political instability?
options: It produced many small parties and weak coalition governments
It gave all power to a single dominant party
It prevented any elections from taking place
It excluded workers from voting
questions.explain: Proportional representation meant no party usually won a majority, leading to fragile, short-lived coalitions.

questions.q: A student notes that Germany's economic recovery after 1924 relied heavily on loans from the United States. Which agreement arranged these loans?
options: The Dawes Plan
The Young Plan
The Locarno Pact
The Treaty of Rapallo
questions.explain: The 1924 Dawes Plan reorganised reparations and provided US loans that helped stabilise the German economy.

questions.q: Why did French and Belgian troops occupy the Ruhr in January 1923?
options: Because Germany had fallen behind on its reparations payments
Because Germany had invaded France
Because the League of Nations ordered it
Because German workers had gone on strike in France
questions.explain: When Germany defaulted on reparations, France and Belgium occupied the Ruhr to seize goods and resources directly.

questions.q: In which year did Hitler attempt the Munich (Beer Hall) Putsch?
questions.explain: The failed Munich Putsch took place in November 1923 during the crisis of hyperinflation and the Ruhr occupation.

questions.q: While imprisoned in Landsberg after the Munich Putsch, Hitler wrote which book?
options: Mein Kampf
The Doctrine of Fascism
Das Kapital
The Twenty-Five Points
questions.explain: Hitler dictated Mein Kampf ('My Struggle') in prison, setting out his ideas on race, living space and dictatorship.

questions.q: How did the 1929 Wall Street Crash help the Nazis gain support?
options: It caused mass unemployment and disillusion with the Weimar government
It made Germany suddenly wealthy and confident
It forced the Nazis to disband temporarily
It led to the return of the Kaiser
questions.explain: The Depression brought soaring unemployment, and many desperate Germans turned to extreme parties like the Nazis.

questions.q: What was a key consequence of the Reichstag Fire in February 1933?
options: Hitler used it to pass an emergency decree suspending civil rights and to arrest Communists
It forced Hitler to resign as Chancellor
It led to free elections that removed the Nazis
It caused Hindenburg to abolish the presidency
questions.explain: Blaming the Communists, Hitler persuaded Hindenburg to issue a decree curbing freedoms and crushing his opponents.

questions.q: What did the Enabling Act of March 1933 allow Hitler to do?
options: Make laws for four years without the consent of the Reichstag
Declare himself Kaiser of Germany
Abolish the German army
Ban the Nazi Party's rivals from voting only in local elections
questions.explain: The Enabling Act let Hitler pass laws without parliament, effectively making him a legal dictator.

questions.q: On the Night of the Long Knives in 1934, why did Hitler order the murder of Ernst Röhm and other SA leaders?
options: To remove a threat to his power and win the support of the army
To punish them for opposing the Enabling Act
To replace them with Communist officials
To end Germany's involvement in the League of Nations
questions.explain: Hitler eliminated the powerful SA leadership to secure his own position and reassure the regular army.

questions.q: Who was the head of the SS in Nazi Germany?
options: Heinrich Himmler
Joseph Goebbels
Hermann Goering
Reinhard Heydrich
questions.explain: Heinrich Himmler led the SS, which controlled the police, concentration camps and much of the Nazi terror system.

questions.q: Who was the Nazi Minister of Propaganda?
options: Joseph Goebbels
Heinrich Himmler
Rudolf Hess
Albert Speer
questions.explain: Joseph Goebbels controlled propaganda, censorship, the media and rallies to shape public opinion in Germany.

questions.q: What did the Nuremberg Laws of 1935 do?
options: Stripped Jews of German citizenship and banned marriage between Jews and non-Jews
Gave Jews equal rights with other Germans
Required all Germans to join the Nazi Party
Banned the Hitler Youth movement
questions.explain: The 1935 Nuremberg Laws removed Jewish citizenship and outlawed marriage or relations between Jews and 'Aryans'.

questions.q: Kristallnacht in November 1938 is best described as what?
options: A state-encouraged wave of violence against Jewish homes, shops and synagogues
A peaceful protest by Jews against Nazi rule
A workers' strike in the Ruhr region
A Nazi festival celebrating the harvest
questions.explain: In the 'Night of Broken Glass', Nazi-organised mobs destroyed Jewish property and attacked Jews across Germany.

questions.q: The Nazi 'Strength Through Joy' (KdF) scheme was designed mainly to achieve what?
options: To keep workers loyal by providing cheap leisure and holidays
To retrain unemployed people as soldiers
To increase church attendance
To reduce the power of the SS
questions.explain: Strength Through Joy offered subsidised holidays and activities to win worker support and discourage opposition.

questions.q: The Nazi slogan 'Kinder, Kuche, Kirche' reflected which policy towards women?
options: Encouraging women to focus on children, the home and church rather than careers
Recruiting women as army officers
Requiring women to run large businesses
Giving women the leading roles in the Nazi Party
questions.explain: The Nazis promoted 'children, kitchen, church', pushing women out of work and towards motherhood and domestic life.

specSource: Cambridge IGCSE History (0470) syllabus; Depth Study: Germany 1918-45
